summary: A status report on FTP implementations and further comments. It lists which hosts have working server and user FTPs, notes that most TENEX servers are nearly identical, and mentions that MIT-Multics has a server that does not listen on socket 3.

eli5.summary: A scoreboard of which computers can already send and receive files with the file-sharing rules, plus a few extra notes.

subtitle: A November 1972 status report on ARPANET FTP implementations, with twelve proposed refinements to the protocol.

tldr.problem: By late 1972 many hosts had working FTP servers and users, but the protocol, as stated in RFC 354 and RFC 385, left several behaviors unclear or awkward.
tldr.mechanism: A. Bhushan reports who had working FTPs and lists twelve suggestions: clearer STAT and LIST replies, new HELP and NLST commands, new reply codes 331 and 433, pathname syntax, record and error-check ideas, and more.
tldr.outcome: The author planned, after comments, to combine RFC 354, RFC 385 and this RFC into a single document issued as the ARPANET Official File Transfer Protocol.

today: RFC 414 updates RFC 385 and, per its header, RFC 354. The unit metadata lists its own status as Unknown, and the text only states a plan to combine the three documents into one official FTP specification.

sections.title: FTP Implementation Status
sections.content:
The RFC reports that a number of hosts have working server and user FTPs. Hosts named as fully functioning include BBN (A and B), SRI-ARC, UTAH, CASE, USC-ISI, CCA, MIT-AI, MIT-Mathlab, MIT-DMCG, CMU, AMES-67 and SU-AI. MIT-Multics has both but its server does not listen on socket 3, and UCSB would soon have them.

The author notes that the user-FTP side is where useful features can go, such as the TENEX "SNDMSG USER@HOST" mail feature, a "TRANS" command at MIT-AI and MIT-ML, and a "Quote" or "talk" mode for typing commands straight to the server. He also notes that transfers between PDP-10s in "Image 36" are an order of magnitude faster than in "ASCII 8".
sections.eli5: First comes a roll call of which computers can already send files, plus some handy tricks people added to their own versions.

sections.title: An Open-Ended Protocol
sections.content:
The suggestions here pertain to FTP as stated in RFC 354 and RFC 385. After comments, the author intends to have the three RFCs combined into a single document and issued as the ARPANET Official File Transfer Protocol.

The RFC stresses that FTP is open-ended, with room for experimentation. New commands, reply codes, data representation types and file structures may be defined. Two sites that agree may define their own experimental set, but such additions should be well documented so other sites can use them.
sections.eli5: The rules are meant to grow. Two friends may invent their own extra moves, as long as they write them down.

sections.title: Commands and Replies
sections.content:
FTP assumes line-at-a-time interaction with local echo. A server is not obliged to provide remote echo and may ignore TELNET control characters, but should not give an error on receiving them. On the TELNET "SYNCH" the server should flush the current command line and wait for input such as "ABOR".

For multi-line output such as STAT, the RFC proposes a "200 status complete" reply to mark the end. A reply to STAT starts with a line beginning 1xx and the following lines must not start with a digit. Responses to STAT go over the TELNET connection and responses to LIST over the data connection; a null argument to LIST lists the current directory.

Two new commands are proposed: HELP and NLST, which sends only file names so a whole directory can be copied. Two reply codes are defined for account handling: "331 Enter Account" when an account is part of login, and "433 Cannot store files without valid account. Enter account." when it is needed only for an operation such as store.
sections.eli5: The note asks servers to say clearly when a long answer is finished, adds a "help" button and a "names only" list, and adds a polite way to ask for an account number.

sections.title: Other Suggestions
sections.content:
Even minimum implementations are urged to accept the TYPE, BYTE, MODE and STRU commands with default values, to avoid ugly error responses. Multiple user names in the MAIL and MLFL commands are strongly urged for server sites.

For pathnames, the RFC floats a standard starting with a special character such as ">" (as in Multics), also used to separate elements, with "'>" as a literal quote. Examples given are >udd>CNet>Doe>foo_bar for Multics, >DSK>JFD>foo bar for ITS and >DOE>foo.bar1 for TENEX.

Other points: an explicit End-of-Record on the last record rather than one implied by End-of-File, extending TELNET synch to BYE and STAT, comments on NOOP, CLSE and SRVR, and two new Block mode descriptor codes to start and end a block check for error detection.
sections.eli5: There are more ideas: accept harmless settings instead of complaining, let one message go to several people, write file paths the same way everywhere, and add a way to spot damaged data.
